description: Calculate voltage, current, resistance, power and energy using the four core circuit equations.
content_html:
Four Equations that Run Every Circuit

Electronics is a practical subject, but behind every circuit there are four mathematical relationships that appear on virtually every exam paper. Master these equations — and the skill of rearranging them — and calculation questions become straightforward. This lesson works through all four with worked examples you can follow step by step.

Ohm’s Law: V = IR

Ohm’s law states that voltage equals current multiplied by resistance:

$$V = IR$$

where V is voltage in volts (V), I is current in amperes (A) and R is resistance in ohms (Ω). Rearranging to make I or R the subject:

$$I = \frac{V}{R} \qquad R = \frac{V}{I}$$

To rearrange, remember the triangle: cover the quantity you want with your thumb and the remaining two show whether to multiply or divide. Always check that your answer is physically sensible — a current of 50 A through a 470 Ω resistor would be unrealistic for a battery circuit and signals a calculation error.

Key Fact

Ohm’s law: \(V = IR\). Rearranged: \(I = V/R\) and \(R = V/I\). V in volts, I in amperes, R in ohms.

Example 1 — find V: A 470 Ω resistor carries 20 mA. What is the voltage across it?

Convert mA to A first: 20 mA = 0.020 A. Then \(V = IR = 0.020 \times 470 = 9.4 \text{ V}\).

Example 2 — find I: A 9 V supply is connected to a 2.2 kΩ resistor. What current flows?

Convert kΩ to Ω: 2.2 kΩ = 2200 Ω. Then \(I = V/R = 9/2200 = 0.00409 \text{ A} = 4.09 \text{ mA}\).

Example 3 — find R: A voltage of 6 V drives a current of 12 mA. What is the resistance?

\(R = V/I = 6/0.012 = 500 \text{ }\Omega\)

Electrical Power: P = IV

Electrical power is the rate of energy transfer. The basic form is:

$$P = IV$$

Combining this with Ohm’s law gives two more forms that are useful when you know only current and resistance, or only voltage and resistance:

$$P = I^2 R \qquad P = \frac{V^2}{R}$$

Power is in watts (W). A component’s power rating (e.g. 0.25 W or 0.5 W for a resistor) must not be exceeded, or it will overheat. You will use \(P = I^2R\) to check whether a chosen resistor’s power rating is sufficient.

Key Fact

Three forms of the power equation: \(P = IV\), \(P = I^2R\), \(P = V^2/R\). Power is in watts (W).

Example 4 — P = IV: A LED circuit draws 20 mA from a 9 V supply. What is the power consumed?

\(P = IV = 0.020 \times 9 = 0.18 \text{ W}\)

Example 5 — check resistor rating: A 470 Ω resistor carries 20 mA. Is a 0.25 W resistor safe?

\(P = I^2R = (0.020)^2 \times 470 = 0.000400 \times 470 = 0.188 \text{ W}\). This is less than 0.25 W, so the resistor is safe.

Example 6 — P = V²/R: A 9 V supply is connected directly across a 100 Ω resistor. What power does it dissipate?

\(P = V^2/R = 81/100 = 0.81 \text{ W}\). A 0.25 W resistor would be destroyed; at least a 1 W rating is required.

Energy Transfer: E = Pt

Energy transfer is calculated when you know how long a device operates:

$$E = Pt$$

where E is energy in joules (J), P is power in watts (W) and t is time in seconds (s). This formula applies to time-on-load contexts: how much energy does a 0.5 W relay consume if it stays energised for 30 seconds?

\(E = Pt = 0.5 \times 30 = 15 \text{ J}\)

Take care with unit prefixes. Milliseconds must be converted to seconds (divide by 1000) and milliamperes to amperes (divide by 1000) before substituting into any equation. A calculation error caused by leaving current in mA instead of A is a common and avoidable mistake.

Linking the Equations Together

The four equations \(V = IR\), \(P = IV\), \(P = I^2R\) and \(P = V^2/R\) are not separate ideas — they are the same relationship rearranged for whichever pair of quantities is given in the question. Choosing the right form first saves both time and arithmetic. If the question gives you voltage and resistance, jump straight to \(P = V^2/R\) rather than first finding the current. If it gives you current and resistance, use \(P = I^2R\). The fastest students never compute an intermediate quantity unless they have to.

A useful sanity check is to keep one eye on the order of magnitude. A household appliance draws watts to kilowatts; a portable LED indicator draws milliwatts to tens of milliwatts; a microcontroller drawing 10 mA from 5 V dissipates \(P = 5 \times 0.01 = 0.05\) W — a tiny fraction of a watt. If your calculator shows several watts for a single resistor in a small signal circuit, you have almost certainly forgotten to convert milliamperes to amperes, or millivolts to volts. Spotting the wrong order of magnitude before writing the final answer recovers marks that would otherwise be lost to a unit slip.
exam_tip_html: Calculation questions award one mark for a correct method or equation and one mark for the correct answer with units. You can earn the method mark even with an arithmetic error, but only if you show the equation clearly. Always convert prefixes before substituting: mA → A (divide by 1000), kΩ → Ω (multiply by 1000), ms → s (divide by 1000). For multi-step calculations, label each step. When asked to check a component’s suitability, state the calculated value AND compare it explicitly to the rated value to earn the evaluation mark.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Ohm’s law: \(V = IR\), rearranged as \(I = V/R\) and \(R = V/I\). Always convert mA to A and kΩ to Ω before substituting.
  • Three power equations: \(P = IV\), \(P = I^2R\), \(P = V^2/R\). Use whichever fits the quantities already known. Power is in watts (W).
  • Energy transfer: \(E = Pt\), where time must be in seconds and power in watts. Used to find total energy consumed by a device over a period of operation.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the correct equation for electrical power when current and resistance are known?
A) P = IV
B) P = V/R
C) P = I²R
D) P = V²I
A resistor has 6 V across it and 30 mA flowing through it. Calculate its resistance.
practice_questions.marks:
\(R = V/I\) [1 mark for correct equation]
Convert: 30 mA = 0.030 A
\(R = 6/0.030 = 200 \text{ }\Omega\) [1 mark for correct answer with unit]

practice_questions.text:
A 9 V battery powers a circuit that draws 45 mA.
(a) Calculate the power consumed by the circuit.
(b) Calculate the energy transferred if the circuit operates for 2 minutes.
practice_questions.marks:
(a) \(P = IV = 0.045 \times 9 = 0.405 \text{ W}\) [1 mark for method; 1 mark for correct answer with unit]
(b) Convert 2 minutes to seconds: 2 × 60 = 120 s. \(E = Pt = 0.405 \times 120 = 48.6 \text{ J}\) [1 mark for method; 1 mark for correct answer with unit — accept 48–49 J]

practice_questions.text: A designer wants to use a 0.25 W resistor of 1 kΩ in a circuit. The current through the resistor is expected to be 18 mA. Determine whether the 0.25 W rating is suitable. Show all working.
practice_questions.marks:
Convert: 18 mA = 0.018 A; 1 kΩ = 1000 Ω [1 mark for correct unit conversion]
\(P = I^2R = (0.018)^2 \times 1000 = 0.000324 \times 1000 = 0.324 \text{ W}\) [1 mark for correct method; 1 mark for correct value]
0.324 W > 0.25 W, so the resistor is NOT suitable at this rating; a 0.5 W or higher rating should be used [1 mark for justified conclusion].

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by Ohm's law and write the equation that expresses it.
practice_questions.marks: Ohm's law states that the voltage across a conductor is directly proportional to the current through it (at constant temperature) [1 mark]. Equation: \(V = IR\) [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: A designer is building a battery-powered alarm system. The system draws 120 mA when active and runs on a 9 V supply. The designer needs to know the total power consumption and whether the energy stored in a 2000 mAh battery is likely to run the system for more than 8 hours continuously. Analyse the situation fully and reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Extended Response: Circuit Analysis and Evaluation
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Correct calculation of power P = IV = 0.120 × 9 = 1.08 W. Correct conversion of battery capacity: 2000 mAh = 2 Ah; energy stored = 2 × 9 = 18 Wh = 64,800 J (or using E = Pt, 1.08 × t = 64,800 J, t = 60,000 s = 16.7 hours). Correct comparison: 16.7 hours > 8 hours, so the battery is adequate. Recognition that real-world factors (internal resistance, temperature, age, non-constant current draw) will reduce actual runtime, so a margin of safety is wise. Justified conclusion that the battery is theoretically sufficient but a higher-capacity battery or low-power mode improves reliability.
Secure: Correct P calculation and valid runtime estimate; comparison to 8-hour requirement correct; some acknowledgment of real-world limitations.
Developing: Correct P calculation; runtime estimate contains unit error or conversion error; conclusion present but limited.
Emerging: P formula attempted with some substitution; conclusion absent or unjustified.

flashcard_questions.a: The equation requires SI units; amperes, not milliamperes.

flashcard_questions.q: A resistor dissipates 0.4 W continuously for 60 seconds. How much energy is transferred?

glossary_terms.definition: The relationship stating that the voltage across a conductor is directly proportional to the current through it, provided temperature remains constant: V = IR.
The rate at which electrical energy is converted to another form of energy, measured in watts (W). P = IV.
The total electrical energy converted by a device, equal to its power multiplied by the time it is switched on: E = Pt, measured in joules (J).
